description: Snowflake ASOF JOIN ... MATCH_CONDITION (...) [ON ...] - the closest-match time-series join. Every expectation was measured on a live Snowflake account with this exact fixture: q(k,t,v) = (1,10,100),(1,20,200),(2,10,300),(3,10,400) and r(k,t,w) = (1,5,1),(1,15,2),(1,25,3),(2,50,4). The join is LEFT OUTER, so unmatched left rows survive null-extended; >= picks the newest earlier right row and <= the oldest later one; a strict comparison excludes the equal row; without an ON clause every right row is a candidate, so the closest match is chosen across the WHOLE right table. A NULL on the match column makes the comparison UNKNOWN, so such a right row is never a candidate. MATCH_CONDITION accepts an expression on either side as long as each side reads only its OWN table - 'r.t <= q.t' is rejected even though it means the same thing - and only the four inequality operators are allowed. It is mandatory, it must PRECEDE the ON clause, and there is no LEFT / RIGHT / INNER ASOF spelling. The right table may be aliased with the words OFFSET and LIMIT, a live quirk found in sqlglot's Snowflake corpus. ASOF and MATCH_CONDITION stay usable as ordinary identifiers. Converted 1:1 from query/AsofJoinTest (now retired); the Java read individual row indexes, which the converted tests state as whole ordered row sets.

CREATE TABLE r (k INTEGER, t INTEGER, w INTEGER)
SELECT q.k, q.t, r.t, r.w FROM q ASOF JOIN r MATCH_CONDITION (q.t >= r.t) ON q.k = r.k ORDER BY q.k, q.t
